Confusable pairs and continuation facts; each block ties to one manual page, and any hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec17-R01 | anchor: A01
Getting a license is often called a modern rite of passage into adulthood, and a dangerous one that demands serious preparation. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec17-R02 | anchor: A01
The graduated license rules call for book learning first and then a minimum amount of supervised driving before solo driving, a sound approach for new drivers of any age. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec17-R03 | anchor: A01
Teaching out loud may lead your learner to offer friendly criticism of your own driving, which you should accept with good humor. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec17-R04 | anchor: A01
Even in early lessons, nothing replaces real experience on the road, but first sessions should focus simply on gaining control of the vehicle. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec17-R05 | anchor: A02
Stay alert as a mentor, anticipating problems and being ready to react to prevent unsafe situations. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec17-R06 | anchor: A02
Do not hit a beginner with everything at once; even a simple right turn involves mirrors, signaling, lane use, braking and turning, so save a first left turn for a calm area. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec17-R07 | anchor: A02
Everything a mentor says is also a distraction for the driver, so keep comments sparing and avoid situations the learner is not ready for. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec17-R08 | anchor: A02
The University of Michigan Transportation Research Institute recommends about 3,000 supervised miles, although each new driver differs. [A02]
Why it matters: group practice amount; confusable recommended miles versus required hours.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec17-R09 | anchor: A02
Track supervised hours in a simple notebook kept in the glove compartment, or copy the manual's sample log. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec17-R10 | anchor: A02
A family driving agreement can cover where and when the teen may drive, how the car is returned, who pays for gas, maintenance and insurance, and the consequences of tickets, damage and moving violations. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec17-R11 | anchor: A02
Alcohol or any other impairment multiplies the crash risk of driving at night with a group of young passengers several times over. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec17-R12 | anchor: A02
Good defensive driving takes more than caution or experience alone; the driver must keep working at good technique after passing the license exam. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec17-R13 | anchor: A03
When teaching a driver whose first language is not English, have the driver study traffic signs and signals thoroughly and help translate them while driving together. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0132]

FACT_ID: sec17-R14 | anchor: A03
Practice the examiner's role by giving simple English instructions such as turn left, slow down or go straight at the next intersection. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0132]

FACT_ID: sec17-R15 | anchor: A03
Most applicants drive at their best during the road test, so passing it does not mean they will keep using safe procedures once the examiner is gone. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0132]
